To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
haemolytic effects are a common feature in the toxicity profiles of a wide variety of chemicals.
haemolytic anemia is a serious toxic effect that can occur after prolonged exposure to chemical compounds.

Haemolytic anemia can occur in rodentic repeated dose toxicity studies and can result in secondary effects, such as renal damage and/or liver enlargement, which may be more sensitive indicators of haemolytically mediated toxicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new, efficient, and sustainable processes for the production of chemicals and materials.
the development of new and more effective methods for the treatment of haemolytically anaemic patients.
the development of a novel method of classification and labelling of chemical substances which induce haemolytic anemia, and is of importance for the European Union and the rest of the world.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
haemolytic effects in the liver, kidney and spleen in the absence of other adverse effects are considered to be non-adverse and therefore do not require classification.
the haemolytic effects observed in the rodent repeated dose studies are not considered to be a significant adverse effect in the context of classification for this endpoint.
haemolytic effects are considered to be a secondary target organ effect in repeated dose toxicity testing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the classification criteria are now in place for haemolyticanemia and that they are in line with the current classification criteria for other endpoints.

the classification criteria proposed in this review are now used in the European Commission's Classification and Labelling (CL) Committee for the classification of substances inducing haemolytis anaemia.

haemolytic anemia is not considered a relevant endpoint for classification for acute toxicity, but that it can be a relevant endpoint in repeated dose toxicity tests and that classification should only be based on haemolytic effects observed in the absence of other effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

haemolytic effects should only be used for classification when they are accompanied by significant changes in clinical pathology parameters, and when they are associated with other signs of systemic toxicity.
haemolytic changes are a toxicological phenomenon and should be assessed as such, not simply a laboratory finding.
haemolytic effects are considered a serious effect in humans, and that the classification criteria for haematotoxicity are based on the severity and reversibility of effects.
